evidence.title: Minusinsk Basin & Boyarskaya Pisanitsa (Middle Yenisei, Siberia): Afanasievo, Okunev & Tagar Bronze–Iron Kurgans
evidence.summary: On the Yenisei steppe oasis enclosed by the Sayan Mountains, Copper/Bronze Age Afanasievo pastoralists, carved Okunev stelae, Andronovo copper miners, and the Iron Age Tagar Scytho-Siberian culture raised thousands of stone-kerbed timber *kurgans* (Salbyk Great Kurgan) and etched log-village/wagon scenes on the Boyarskaya Pisanitsa cliffside.
evidence.limits: Dates bracket the Afanasievo-through-Tagar succession in the Minusinsk Depression prior to Tashtyk–Yenisei Kyrgyz transitions.
evidence.dateBasis: Tagar kurgan dendrochronology and radiocarbon determinations from the Yenisei valley.

evidence.title: Ust-Polui Sanctuary & Lower Ob Tundra (Salekhard, Subarctic Siberia): permafrost carvings & arctic craft (c. 300 BCE–300 CE)
evidence.summary: Permafrost on a bluff overlooking the Ob delta preserved wooden bowls, birchbark quivers, bronze steppe-style plaques, domesticated dog sacrifices/harnesses, and carved antler spoons at the fortified sanctuary of Ust-Polui, revealing long-distance iron and bronze networks reaching the Arctic Circle in Iron Age Western Siberia.
evidence.limits: Coordinate marks modern Salekhard on the Ob River near the Arctic Circle.
evidence.dateBasis: Tree-ring and radiocarbon chronology of Ust-Polui permafrost sacrificial ditches.

evidence.title: Lake Baikal & Upper Lena–Orkhon Corridor: Kitoi–Glazkovo, Xiongnu Ivolga & Kurykan Rock Art
evidence.summary: Around Lake Baikal and the Selenga Valley, the fortified northern Xiongnu trading-and-metalworking frontier town of Ivolga (near Ulan-Ude) gave way in early medieval centuries to the Kurykan culture—known from dry-stone Olkhon forts, Old Turkic runiform inscriptions, and Shishkino sandstone horseman petroglyphs—ancestral to later Buryat and Sakha (Yakut) pastoralists.
evidence.limits: Broad 13-century window tracks Xiongnu frontier urbanization through early medieval Kurykan rock-art horizons.
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon-dated Ivolga ramparts, Olkhon Iron Age burials, and Lena–Baikal cultural stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Isker (Qashliq), Tobolsk & Lena Ostrog Corridor: Khanate of Sibir & 17th–19th c. Frontier Siberia
evidence.summary: Centered at Qashliq (Isker) near Tobolsk along the Irtysh, the Siberian Tatar Khanate of Sibir (ruled by Kuchum Khan before Yermak's Cossack expedition of 1581–1585) controlled West Siberian fur networks later reorganized into Tsarist Russian sable-*yasak* river forts stretching via Mangazeya and Tobolsk to Yakutsk (founded 1632 in Sakha homeland) and Trans-Siberian rail links in the 1890s.
evidence.limits: Single Tobolsk–Irtysh anchor stands for multiple Indigenous Ob-Ugric, Selkup, Samoyed, Evenki, Sakha, and Tsarist administrative shifts.
evidence.dateBasis: Tatar Isker strata, Siberian chronicles (1581–1587), and Tobolsk stone kremlin archives.

evidence.title: Issyk Kurgan & Berel Frozen Tombs (Jetysu / Altai, Kazakhstan): Saka 'Golden Warrior' & Steppe Horsemen
evidence.summary: In the Tian Shan foothills east of Almaty (Jetysu), the 5th–4th c. BCE Issyk burial mound preserved over 4,000 stamped gold plaques alongside a tall conical headdress and a silver bowl incised with 26 un-deciphered runiform/Kharoshthi-linked signs, while Wusun/Saka–Yuezhi successors built extensive valley cemeteries and permafrost horse-sacrifice tombs at Berel in the Kazakh Altai.
evidence.limits: Ongoing debates examine the script on the Issyk silver cup and precise gender/dynastic status of the buried individual.
evidence.dateBasis: Dendrochronology and radiocarbon dating from Issyk, Berel kurgan 11, and Jetysu Saka-Wusun complexes.

evidence.title: Taraz, Otrar & Balasagun (Kazakhstan–Kyrgyzstan): Talas (751 CE), Qarakhanid Steppe Cities & Silk Routes
evidence.summary: Across the Chu and Talas valleys of northern Central Asia, Sogdian merchant colonies under the Western Turkic Khaganate founded Suyab and Taraz (site of the 751 CE Battle of Talas between Tang Chinese and Abbasid–Tibetan coalitions), flourishing later under the bilingual Turkic–Islamic Qarakhanid Khanate (Aisha Bibi mausoleum, Burana minaret) and Golden Horde/Timurid oasis urbanism before Otrar declined after Timur's death in 1405 CE.
evidence.limits: Taraz coordinate marks the Talas–Chu urbanized steppe belt east toward Suyab.
evidence.dateBasis: Suyab/Taraz Sogdian–Turkic coin sequences, Qarakhanid brick masonry, and 751 CE Tang–Abbasid synchronization.

evidence.title: Saraychik & Golden Horde Steppe Cities (Lower Ural River, Western Kazakhstan): Jochid Caravan Crossroads
evidence.summary: Perched where caravans ferried across the Ural River linking Lower Volga Sarai capitals to Khwarazm and the Kazakh steppe, Saraychik (Saray-Jük) evolved from a Jochid/Golden Horde administrative mint town with underfloor heating (*kan*) and glazed mosaic baths into the 15th–16th century capital of the Nogai Horde and early Kazakh Khanate until Cossack raids damaged the site around 1580.
evidence.limits: Ural River meander erosion washed away portions of the central citadel prior to rescue excavations.
evidence.dateBasis: Golden Horde Jochid silver/copper coin series (13th–14th c.) and 16th-century Kazakh/Nogai chronicles.

evidence.title: Turkistan / Yasi (Southern Kazakhstan): Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi & Kazakh Khanate Political Seat
evidence.summary: Rebuilt by Timur starting in 1389 CE around the tomb of Sufi poet Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, Yasi (modern Turkistan) became both a major spiritual shrine of Central Asian Turkic peoples and the long-standing political and burial seat of the Kazakh Khanate's Khans and *biys* (such as Tauke Khan and Ablai Khan across the Senior, Middle, and Junior *Zhüz*) prior to Kokand and 1860s Russian Imperial expansion.
evidence.limits: Pastoral Kazakh seasonal migration pastures extended thousands of kilometers north of Syr Darya winter oasis capitals.
evidence.dateBasis: 1397–1399 CE Timurid foundation bronze cauldron/epigraphy and 16th–19th century Kazakh–Russian–Central Asian records.

evidence.title: Tabon / Manunggul Cave & Ayub Cave (Palawan & Mindanao, Philippines): Nephrite Jade & Burial-Jar Seas
evidence.summary: Radiocarbon and artifact sourcing in Philippine caves—from Palawan's sculpted spirit-boat lid on the Manunggul Jar (~890–710 BCE) and Taiwan Fengtian nephrite *lingling-o* ear ornaments to South Cotabato's anthropomorphic terracotta jars at Ayub Cave—reveal vibrant Metal Age South China Sea maritime craft and funerary complexity bridging Taiwan, Vietnam (Sa Huynh), and Borneo.
evidence.limits: Palawan coordinate locates the Tabon–Manunggul limestone karst peninsula while jar burials span Batanes to Mindanao.
evidence.dateBasis: Manunggul Cave jar radiocarbon determinations, obsidian/nephrite geochemical sourcing, and Ayub terracotta seriations.

evidence.title: Laguna Copperplate (900 CE) & Butuan Balangay Ships (Luzon & Mindanao): Literacy, Gold & Srivijayan Trade
evidence.dateLabel: c. 750–1350 CE (LCI exact date: 21 April 900 CE)
evidence.summary: On 21 April 900 CE (Shaka 822), the Laguna Copperplate Inscription—written in Old Kawi script blending Old Malay, Sanskrit, Old Javanese, and Old Tagalog—acquitted Namwaran of a gold debt around Manila Bay and Bulacan. Simultaneously in northeastern Mindanao, coastal chiefdoms at Butuan built nine plank-lashed ocean-going *balangay* boats (320–1250 CE), worked alluvial gold ornaments, and dispatched direct tribute missions to Song China (1001–1011 CE).
evidence.limits: Laguna Bay and Butuan were distinct Luzon and Mindanao riverine polities sharing maritime literacy and Southeast Asian metal networks.
evidence.dateBasis: Astronomically verified Shaka 822 date on the Laguna Copperplate and radiocarbon-dated Butuan balangay hull timbers.

evidence.title: Ifugao Cordillera Rice Terraces (Northern Luzon, Philippines): Highland Hydraulic Engineering & Autonomy
evidence.summary: Carved along dizzying 70-degree mountain slopes across Ifugao and Kalinga above managed *muyong* cloud forests that capture rainwater into stone-walled pond fields, the Cordillera terraces showcase indigenous communal hydrology—with recent excavations at Old Kiyyangan showing rapid wet-rice and pig feasting expansion as Igorot communities actively resisted Spanish colonial subjugation.
evidence.limits: While oral traditions speak of millennia of antiquity, systematic excavations in Kiangan/Ifugao establish peak wet-rice terrace construction primarily from ~1000–1600 CE onward.
evidence.dateBasis: Ifugao Archaeological Project radiocarbon/phytolith trench dates and UNESCO Cordillera terrace documentation.

evidence.title: Sulu Sultanate, Ternate–Tidore & Manila Galleon Port (Wallacea–Philippines, 1450–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Connecting Maluku's sole clove-producing volcanic sultanates of Ternate and Tidore north across the Sulu–Mindanao Sultanates (Jolo, Maguindanao) to Manila—founded from Rajah Sulayman's Tagalog-Bruneian port into Spain's Intramuros hub of the 1565–1815 Manila–Acapulco silver-for-silk galleons—Archipelagic Southeast Asia sat at the nexus of global silver, spice, tripang, and Islamic/Catholic encounters through the 1898 Philippine Revolution.
evidence.limits: Spain's Intramuros controlled Manila, Cebu, and coastal Visayan towns while Sulu and Maguindanao maintained sovereign maritime sultanates until the late 19th century.
evidence.dateBasis: 15th-century Sulu royal *tarsila* chronicles, Spanish Manila galleon customs ledgers, and Dutch–Ternate treaties.

evidence.title: Budj Bim & Tae Rak Cultural Landscape (Gunditjmara Country, SW Victoria, Australia): 6,600-year stone eel traps
evidence.dateLabel: c. 4650 BCE–1900 CE (UNESCO oldest dated channels ~6,600 yr)
evidence.summary: Gunditjmara Traditional Owners engineered kilometers of basalt channels, weirs, and holding ponds across the Tyrendarra lava flow of Budj Bim and Lake Condah (Tae Rak) to herd, trap, and smoke *kooyang* short-finned eels (*Anguilla australis*) year-round—sustaining permanent circular basalt-walled village huts millennia before settler dispossession and ongoing heritage resurgence.
evidence.limits: While deep channels date back ~6,600 years, detailed redevelopment phases at Muldoons Trap complex concentrate around the past 800–2,000 years.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO inscription dossier radiocarbon channel sediment dates and Gunditjmara–Monash excavation stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Ngunnhu / Brewarrina Fish Traps & Murray–Darling Gathering Corridors (NSW, Australia)
evidence.summary: Along a rocky bar of the Barwon–Darling River sacred to Ngemba, Wailwan, Yuwaalaraay, Kamilaroi, and neighboring nations (attributed in Dreaming law to Baiame and his sons Booma-ooma-nowi and Ghinda-inda-mui), half a kilometer of dry-stone interlocking rock pens adjusted dynamically with river levels to harvest seasonal native cod and perch runs during inter-tribal ceremonies.
evidence.limits: Flood rearrangements make bare basalt boulders notoriously difficult to date directly by radiocarbon alone; persistence across centuries is verified by ethnohistory and riverine archaeology.
evidence.dateBasis: Ethnohistorical accounts, riverine shelter archaeology, and comparative Aboriginal aquaculture chronologies.

evidence.title: Arnhem Land–Kimberley Maritime Encounters: Yolŋu & Macassan Trepang Fleets (c. 1640–1907 CE)
evidence.summary: Sailing southeast on the northwest monsoon (*bara*) from Makassar in Sulawesi long before British fleets reached Sydney, Bugis–Makassar *perahu* crews set up stone boiling hearths (*bepang*) across Arnhem Land and Groote Eylandt to process sea cucumber (*trepang*/*bêche-de-mer*) with Yolŋu partners—leaving tamarind trees, iron knives, dugout *lippa-lippa* canoes, Dutch coins, rock-art ships, shared loanwords, and deep kinship ties.
evidence.limits: Radiocarbon dates on beeswax rock art (Djuliwadj) and hearth charcoal support mid-17th-century contact alongside documented 1720s–1906 fleets.
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon dating of Arnhem trepang processing hearths and Dutch East India Company Macassan shipping notices.

evidence.title: Lutruwita / Tasmania: 12,000-Year Bass Strait Separation, Kelp Crafts & Frontier Survival (10,000 BCE–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Cut off from mainland Australia when post-glacial sea rise flooded Bass Strait (~12,000–10,000 BCE), nine Palawa nations (including oyster-harvesting and abalone-diving coastal clans around Rocky Cape, West Point, and Oyster Bay) sustained open grasslands with cultural fire regimes and bark/reed catamarans—experiencing severe colonial frontier violence during the Black War (1824–1832) yet enduring through vibrant Bass Strait and Palawa communities into 1900 and today.
evidence.limits: Reiterates survival of Palawa lineages rather than colonial-era 'extinction' myths long discredited in modern Australian scholarship.
evidence.dateBasis: Tasmanian Holocene midden sequences (West Point, Rocky Cape) and 19th-century archival/oral community history.

evidence.title: Gochang, Hwasun & Ganghwa Megalithic Dolmens (Korean Peninsula): Bronze Age Table & Capstone Cemeteries
evidence.summary: Containing nearly 40% of all documented Bronze Age megalithic dolmens worldwide (tens of thousands across the peninsula, epitomized by UNESCO's Gochang, Hwasun, and Ganghwa clusters), Korean Mumun Bronze Age rice-farming chiefdoms quarried multi-ton granite capstones paired with mandolin-shaped bronze daggers (*bipahyeong donggeom*), ground stone daggers, and burnished red pottery associated with Gojoseon and Jin regional polities.
evidence.limits: Individual dolmen clusters vary widely in chronology between earlier northern table types and southern capstone types.
evidence.dateBasis: Mumun period radiocarbon dates, Liaoning/Korean bronze dagger typologies, and UNESCO dolmen quarry documentation.

evidence.title: Gyeongju (Seorabeol), Buyeo & Goguryeo: Korean Three Kingdoms Gold Crowns, Kilns & Seokguram (57 BCE–935 CE)
evidence.summary: Between Goguryeo's cliff fortresses and tomb murals in the north, Baekje's refined gilt-bronze incense burners across Gongju/Buyeo, and Silla's royal capital at Gyeongju—preserving immense timber-chamber mound tombs stuffed with antler-motif gold crowns, Roman/Mediterranean glasswork, Cheomseongdae observatory (7th c.), and Unified Silla's granite grotto at Seokguram and Bulguksa Temple—the Three Kingdoms forged enduring Korean political, Buddhist, and artistic foundations.
evidence.limits: Traditional 57 BCE founding date in Samguk Sagi precedes clearest archaeological Silla state mounds (3rd–6th c. CE).
evidence.dateBasis: Archaeological tomb seriation in Daereungwon/Gyeongju, Cheomseongdae & Seokguram UNESCO records, and Gwanggaeto Stele (414 CE).

evidence.title: Gaeseong (Songdo) & Haeinsa (Goryeo Dynasty, 918–1392 CE): Celadon, Tripitaka Koreana & Movable Metal Type (1234/1377)
evidence.summary: Centered at Gaeseong's cosmically planned royal citadel Manwoldae while trading via Byeongnando port with Song, Jurchen, and Arab merchants (coining the Western name 'Korea'), Goryeo artisans perfected inlaid kingfisher-green *cheongja* celadon, carved the 81,258 woodblocks of the *Tripitaka Koreana* (preserved intact at Haeinsa) during 13th-century Mongol resistance, and printed the world's oldest surviving movable-metal-type book (*Jikji*, 1377 CE).
evidence.limits: Gaeseong anchor places the Goryeo capital while Haeinsa Monastery preserves the Tripitaka blocks in South Gyeongsang.
evidence.dateBasis: Manwoldae excavations, Tripitaka woodblock colophons (1236–1251 CE), and 1377 Cheongju Jikji colophon.

evidence.title: Hanyang / Seoul (Joseon Dynasty, 1392–1900 CE): Royal Palaces, Hangul Alphabet (1446) & Rain-Gauge Hydrology
evidence.summary: Relocating the capital inside Seoul's mountain wall in 1394 CE, Joseon Korea built Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces, engineered Jang Yeong-sil's standardized rain gauges (*cheugugi*, 1441 CE) and turtle ships against the 1592–1598 Imjin invasions, and under King Sejong's Hall of Worthies promulgated *Hunminjeongeum* (1446 CE)—the phonological Hangul alphabet designed from vocal-organ geometry—while producing vast *Veritable Records* (*Joseon Wangjo Sillok*) through the 1897 Korean Empire.
evidence.limits: Early palace wings rebuilt after late-16th and 19th-century fires retain traditional layout plans.
evidence.dateBasis: 1394 Seoul layout archives, 1446 Hunminjeongeum woodblock edition, and complete Joseon Wangjo Sillok annals.

evidence.title: Areni-1 Cave, Kura-Araxes & Trialeti Kurgans (Armenia & Georgia): Winepress (4100 BCE) & Royal Goldsmithing
evidence.summary: Cool dry microclimates inside Vayots Dzor's Areni-1 Cave (Armenia) preserved a ~4100–4000 BCE crushed-grape vinting installation and the oldest known leather shoe (~3500 BCE), flanked by highland Kura-Araxes red-black burnished pottery villages and lavish Middle Bronze Age Trialeti royal timber-chamber kurgans (southern Georgia) stuffed with granulated gold goblets and silver cauldrons.
evidence.limits: Coordinate marks Areni-1 Cave along the Arpa River valley in Armenia; Trialeti kurgans lie in southern Georgia.
evidence.dateBasis: Accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dates on Areni leather shoe/grape seeds and Kura-Araxes/Trialeti graves.

evidence.title: Tushpa (Van) & Erebuni Citadel (Urartu / Armenia): Volcanic-Stone Water Canals & Fortresses (860–585 BCE)
evidence.summary: Centered around Lake Van (Tushpa) and expanding across the Armenian Highlands into Arin Berd/Erebuni (founded 782 BCE by King Argishti I—root of the name Yerevan), Urartu rivaled Neo-Assyria with cyclopean basalt fortresses, the 51-km Menua irrigation aqueduct, polychrome citadel frescoes, storage pithoi vineyards (*Teishebaini*/*Karmir Blur*), and bronze helmets and cauldrons traded far into Greece and Etruria.
evidence.limits: Erebuni coordinate anchors Yerevan's Urartian northern stronghold complementary to Tushpa around Lake Van.
evidence.dateBasis: 782 BCE Argishti I foundation basalt cuneiform slab at Erebuni and Urartian royal canal inscriptions.

evidence.title: Etchmiadzin, Mtskheta & Vani (Armenia & Caucasian Iberia/Colchis): Iron–Classical Cross-Caucasus States
evidence.summary: From Colchian Vani's golden burials and classical temple terraces on the Black Sea approach to Mtskheta (capital of Caucasian Iberia with Pompey-era and bilingual Armazi Greek–Aramaic inscriptions) and Etchmiadzin—central sanctuary of Armenia's early-4th-century Christianization, Mesrop Mashtots's 405 CE alphabet, and 7th-century central-domed tetraconch church architecture at Zvartnots—the South Caucasus linked Mediterranean, Persian, and steppe worlds.
evidence.limits: Coordinate marks Vagharshapat/Etchmiadzin; Colchian Vani and Iberian Mtskheta stand north in Georgia.
evidence.dateBasis: UNESCO Etchmiadzin & Zvartnots stratigraphy, 4th–5th c. epigraphy, and Vani/Mtskheta excavation phases.

evidence.title: Ani, Tbilisi & Derbent (Bagratid Armenia, Georgian Golden Age & Caspian Gates, 900–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Above the Akhurian River canyon, Bagratid capital Ani earned renown as the 'City of 1001 Churches' around Trdat's ribbed-pier Cathedral (1001 CE) and Silk Road arched bridges, while Queen Tamar's 12th–13th century Georgian Golden Age (Vardzia, Gelati, Tbilisi's multi-faith baths and mosques/churches) and Sasanian–Islamic fortified Derbent anchored the Caucasus transit through Ottoman, Safavid, Qajar, and Russian Imperial centuries to 1900.
evidence.limits: Ani saw devastating earthquakes and depopulation after the 14th century while Tbilisi remained the continuous political hub of eastern Georgia.
evidence.dateBasis: Dated Armenian/Georgian building inscriptions at Ani and Tbilisi alongside UNESCO heritage dossiers.

evidence.title: Ban Chiang (Khorat Plateau) & Cổ Loa (Red River Delta): Bronze–Dong Son Drums & Wet-Rice Citadel
evidence.summary: On northeast Thailand's Khorat Plateau, Ban Chiang's long cemetery and settlement sequence traces early upland metallurgy and iconic spiral-painted pottery, complemented in northern Vietnam's Red River Delta by the Đông Sơn bronze-drum tradition and the massive concentric rammed-earth ramparts and bronze crossbow-bolt caches of the Âu Lạc citadel at Cổ Loa (3rd–2nd c. BCE) prior to Han expansion.
evidence.limits: AMS radiocarbon revisions tightened Ban Chiang's earliest bronze levels to ~11th–10th c. BCE while Neolithic basal levels extend earlier.
evidence.dateBasis: AMS dating of Ban Chiang skeletal/rice-chaff samples and Co Loa rampart/bronze arrow trench stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Plain of Jars (Xiangkhoang, Laos): Carved Sandstone Megalithic Mortuary Complexes (c. 1200 BCE–500 CE)
evidence.summary: Dotting over 90 upland clearings in northeastern Laos, thousands of hollowed sandstone jars weighing up to 14 tonnes—recently illuminated by OSL, U/Pb zircon, and radiocarbon research revealing secondary skeletal burials, ceramic burial jars (*death jars*), glass beads, and iron goods around carved megaliths—demonstrate complex highland mortuary social landscapes connecting river basins across interior Mainland Southeast Asia.
evidence.limits: Dating of jar quarrying vs. subsequent surrounding mortuary deposits (c. 1240 BCE–13th c. CE ritual reuse) distinguishes carving from later interments.
evidence.dateBasis: Recent OSL, radiocarbon, and U/Pb zircon studies at Sites 1, 2, and 52 plus UNESCO WHC dossier.

evidence.title: Mỹ Sơn (Champa) & Thăng Long (Hanoi, Vietnam): Hindu–Buddhist Maritime Champa & Independent Đại Việt (400–1858 CE)
evidence.summary: Inside an enclosed central-Vietnamese mountain valley near Hội An, Hindu brick sanctuary towers of Mỹ Sơn (with the ~4th-century Đông Yên Châu Old Cham inscription—oldest attested Austronesian text—honoring Bhadreśvara) balanced the Red River kingdom of Đại Việt centered from 1010 CE at Thăng Long (Hanoi's Imperial Citadel), which defeated three Yuan-Mongol invasions (1258–1288) and pioneered glazed Chu Đậu trade ceramics across Maritime Asia.
evidence.limits: Representative Mỹ Sơn coordinate covers central Champa while Red River Đại Việt centered farther north at Thăng Long (21.03°N).
evidence.dateBasis: 4th–13th century Sanskrit/Old Cham epigraphy at My Son and UNESCO Thang Long/My Son excavations.

evidence.title: Luang Prabang (Lan Xang), Chiang Mai (Lan Na) & Ayutthaya: Mekong–Chao Phraya Kingdoms (1350–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Across the interior river valleys of Thailand, Laos, and Shan uplands, Fa Ngum founded Lan Xang ('Million Elephants') at Luang Prabang (1353 CE) alongside Mangrai's Lan Na (Chiang Mai, 1296 CE) and the cosmopolite port-empire of Ayutthaya (1351–1767 CE)—hosting Japanese, Persian, Dutch, and French envoys before Konbaung wars, Bangkok's Chakri Chakravartin state (1782), and French Indochina rivalries partitioned mainland borders by 1900.
evidence.limits: Ayutthaya and Luang Prabang formed interconnected mandala networks rather than rigid centralized nation-states.
evidence.dateBasis: 1351/1353 CE royal foundation chronicles, palm-leaf *tamnan* archives, and diplomatic mission records.

evidence.title: Staraya Ladoga & Veliky Novgorod (NW Rus'): Viking-Slavic River Entrepôt & Birchbark Literacy (753–1478 CE)
evidence.summary: Dendro-dated timber workshops from 753 CE at Staraya Ladoga (the multiethnic Finnic–Slavic–Scandinavian gateway into the Volkhov–Dnieper 'Varangians to Greeks' route) fed the rise of Novgorod, whose waterlogged wooden streets yielded over 1,100 ordinary medieval birchbark letters (*beresty*—including child Onfim's school exercises and women's legal notes) alongside Veche republic Hanseatic fur trade until Muscovite absorption in 1478.
evidence.limits: Birchbark preservation depends on anaerobic urban clay deposits concentrated in Novgorod and Staraya Russa.
evidence.dateBasis: Continuous annual Novgorod timber dendrochronology (753 CE Ladoga oak to 15th-century street pavings) and birchbark paleography.

evidence.title: Kyiv (St. Sophia Cathedral & Podil, Dnieper): Kyivan Rus' Metropolis & 988 Christianization (880–1240 CE)
evidence.summary: Dominating Dnieper river commerce linking Baltic Scandinavia to Constantinople and the Volga (complementing Khazar and Bolgar trade), Kyivan Rus' adopted Byzantine Christianity under Volodymyr the Great (988 CE), codified *Ruska Pravda* law under Yaroslav the Wise, raised the gilded mosaic Cathedral of Saint-Sophia (founded 1037 CE) with multilingual churchyard graffiti, and minted gold/silver *zlatniks* prior to Batu Khan's 1240 Mongol siege.
evidence.limits: Late-11th–12th century Kyivan principalities increasingly functioned as a dynastic federation of semi-independent Rus' principalities.
evidence.dateBasis: Dendro-dated Podil timber log houses, 1037 CE Saint-Sophia foundation mosaics, and *Primary Chronicle* annals.

evidence.title: Vladimir–Suzdal, Tver & Moscow (Oka–Volga Mesopotamia): White-Stone Principalities to Russian Empire (1100–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Rebounding in the forest northeast around carved limestone churches at Vladimir and Bogolyubovo (1158–1165 CE) under Andrei Bogolyubsky, Muscovy gradually unified Oka–Volga principalities through Golden Horde *yarlyk* tax diplomacy (1240s–1480 Ugra Stand), Ivan III's Kremlin rebuild, Peter the Great's 1703 St. Petersburg Baltic window, serf emancipation (1861), and industrialization to 1900.
evidence.limits: Single Vladimir coordinate anchors the Volga–Oka core that expanded into Moscow and Imperial St. Petersburg.
evidence.dateBasis: 12th-century Vladimir limestone relief epigraphy, Golden Horde *yarlyk* charters, and Russian Imperial census archives.

evidence.title: Kernavė, Vilnius & Riga (Eastern Baltic): Hillfort Federation & Grand Duchy of Lithuania (1000–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Protected by five steep Neris-valley earthen hillforts at UNESCO-listed Kernavė, Baltic Aukštaitian and Samogitian dukes forged the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Mindaugas (crowned 1253 CE) and Gediminas (founding tolerant multilingual Vilnius in 1323 CE)—extending from the Baltic to the Black Sea in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth while preserving Europe's last state-level pre-Christian traditions until 1387/1413.
evidence.limits: Later medieval Union of Lublin (1569) and 1795 Partitions reshaped Vilnius inside Tsarist borderlands through 1900.
evidence.dateBasis: Kernave stratified Pajauta valley excavations and 1323 CE Gediminas Latin diplomatic letters.

evidence.title: House of Taga (Tinian) & Marianas Latte Villages: 3,500-Year Austronesian Settlement to Latte Architecture
evidence.dateLabel: c. 1500 BCE–1700 CE (Latte Phase c. 900–1700 CE)
evidence.summary: Settled directly across 2,300+ km of open Philippine Sea waters around 1500 BCE by red-slipped pottery navigators, CHamoru communities across Guam, Tinian, Saipan, and Rota transitioned after ~900 CE to erecting paired coral-limestone pillars (*haligi*) topped by hemispherical capstones (*tasa*) supporting elevated timber houses—culminating in Tinian's colossal 5.5-metre House of Taga quarry stones prior to Spanish-CHamoru wars (1668–1695).
evidence.limits: Early 1500 BCE pottery horizons predate monumental stone *latte* pillars by more than two millennia.
evidence.dateBasis: Marianas redware AMS dating (~1500 BCE) and Latte Period pillar-foundation charcoal stratigraphy.

evidence.title: Babeldaob Earthworks & Rock Islands (Palau, Western Micronesia): Monumental Crowned Ridges & Stone Villages
evidence.summary: Following colonization by ~1000 BCE, Palauan builders on volcanic Babeldaob carved entire ridges into monumental stepped earth terraces, steep flat-topped earthen crowns (*ked*), and sunken ditches between c. 400 BCE and 800 CE for fortification, ritual display, and taro cultivation—later reorganizing into paved basalt stonework *bai* meeting-house villages tied to Yapese aragonite *rai* stone-money quarries.
evidence.limits: Acidic volcanic clay degrades delicate organics outside shell-bearing coastal middens and Rock Island limestone caves.
evidence.dateBasis: Babeldaob Compact Road archaeological mitigation radiocarbon dates across carved crowns and stonework villages.

evidence.title: Chief Roi Mata's Domain (Efate, Vanuatu) & Lapita–Mangasi–Fiji Chiefdoms: Living Oral Memory in Stone
evidence.dateLabel: c. 1000 BCE–1900 CE (Roi Mata c. 1600 CE)
evidence.summary: From Lapita potters at Teouma (~1000 BCE) through the Kuwae volcanic eruption of ~1452 CE, Vanuatu oral traditions remember Paramount Chief Roi Mata uniting warring Efate clans under the peace-making *naflak* matrilineal festival system around 1600 CE—whose sacred burial island of Artok (Retoka) excavated in 1967 by Garanger stunningly matched local oral accounts down to his posture, conch shell trumpets, and volcanic-ash stratigraphy.
evidence.limits: Artok Island and Fels Cave remain sacred *tapu* landscapes protected by Ni-Vanuatu communities.
evidence.dateBasis: Excavated collective burial layers at Retoka/Mangaas matching post-Kuwae pumice horizons and radiocarbon dates (~1600 CE).

evidence.title: Marshall Islands (*Mattang*/*Rebbelib*) Wave Navigation & Kiribati *Maneaba* Meeting-House Atolls
evidence.summary: Mastering life across razor-thin coral atolls scarcely 2 metres above sea level (settled by ~0–200 CE), Marshallese *ri-meto* navigators mapped ocean-swell refraction, reflection, and interference nodes between low atolls onto coconut-frond stick charts (*mattang*, *rebbelib*) memorized before sailing outrigger *korkor* and *walap* canoes—matched southward in Kiribati's coral-stone *maneaba* council polity up through 19th-century copra and protectorate treaties.
evidence.limits: No physical pre-19th-century stick charts survive from perishable palm midribs; atoll settlement timing rests on excavated pit-taro and midden charcoal.
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon basal atoll habitation layers on Majuro/Laura and ethnographic navigational treatises documented before 1900.

evidence.title: Gajiganna, Zilum & Daima (Lake Chad Clay Plains): Pastoralists, Walled Towns & Sao Civilization (1800 BCE–1500 CE)
evidence.summary: As Mega-Lake Chad retreated across fertile *firki* clay plains, cattle-and-pearl-millet pastoralists at Gajiganna transitioned by c. 500 BCE into huge moated and earthen-walled proto-urban settlements like Zilum (up to 12 hectares) and deeply stratified mound cities like Daima (yielding early iron by c. 4th–5th c. CE), feeding the renowned Sao terracotta-sculpting riverine communities south of Lake Chad.
evidence.limits: Water-table erosion and regional insecurity restrict wide-area excavations across many *firki* tells.
evidence.dateBasis: Radiocarbon stratigraphic columns across Daima I–III and Frankfurt–Maiduguri Gajiganna/Zilum surveys.

evidence.title: Njimi & Birni Gazargamu (Kanem–Bornu Empire, Lake Chad Basin): Trans-Saharan Fezzan Crossroads (800–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Controlling the shortest trans-Saharan salt-horse-copper highway straight north via Kawar Oasis to the Fezzan/Tripoli, the Sayfawa Dynasty ruled Kanem east of Lake Chad from Njimi—adopting Islam by ~1075–1085 CE under Mai Hummay—before relocating west of the lake to build the massive baked-brick walled capital Birni Gazargamu (c. 1484–1808) and flourishing under Mai Idris Alooma and al-Kanemi's Kukawa through Rabih az-Zubayr's 1890s wars.
evidence.limits: Baked-brick foundations mark Birni Gazargamu (Yobe Valley, Nigeria) while medieval Njimi's exact mound east of Lake Chad remains debated.
evidence.dateBasis: Royal *Girgam* king-lists, Ibn Furtu's 16th-c. Borno chronicles, and Birni Gazargamu brick-ruin excavations.

evidence.title: Ouara & Massenya (Sultanates of Wadai & Bagirmi, Chad): Sahelian Statecraft & Trade Corridors (1500–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: East and southeast of Lake Chad, the Sultanate of Bagirmi along the Chari River (Massenya, c. 1522 CE) and the formidable Sultanate of Wadai—ruling from the fortified sandstone palace-mosque capital of Ouara (Wara) in eastern Chad's Abéché hills before shifting to Abéché—opened the direct eastern trans-Saharan desert route via Kufra to Benghazi in the 19th century, fiercely contesting French colonial expansion past 1900.
evidence.limits: Surviving stone-and-fired-brick palace ruins at Ouara anchor a wider savanna confederation of Maba and Arabic-speaking groups.
evidence.dateBasis: 17th–19th century Wadai chronicles, Nachtigal's 1873 Abéché observations, and Ouara palace masonry.

evidence.title: Uri, Ain Farah & El Fasher (Jebel Marra & Fur Sultanate, Darfur, Sudan): Stone Palaces & 40-Day Road (1200–1900 CE)
evidence.summary: Anchored around the volcanic massif of Jebel Marra in western Sudan, the Daju and Tunjur stone-walled mountain capitals of Ain Farah and Uri (yielding red-brick mosques, terraced palaces, and Red Sea/Nile imports) evolved by the 17th century into the Keira Sultanate of Darfur (Sulayman Solongdungo, centered at Kobbei and El Fasher from 1791), dispatching massive camel caravans north along the *Darb al-Arbaʿīn* ('Forty-Day Road') directly to Asyut in Egypt.
evidence.limits: Darb al-Arba'in caravan tolls and regional diplomacy preserved Darfur's sovereignty under Sultan Ali Dinar past 1900 (annexed 1916).
evidence.dateBasis: Darfur survey pottery, fired-brick architectural phases at Uri/Ain Farah, and Keira sultanate chancery documents (*hakura* land charters).
